answers.text:
My dear friend,

Even if both choices — to move away or to stay — brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the choice to remain near one's relatives.

Why? Because I believe that the ties of kinship are not merely useful, but sacred. They are the foundation upon which a man builds his life, and they are the first and surest source of love and support.

I do not say that moving away is without its merits. I have seen men who have done so and have done well, and I have seen them return with new wisdom and new strength. But I have also seen men who, once they left, never returned, and I have seen the homes they left behind grow quiet and empty.

If both paths lead to equal success, then the choice is not one of right or wrong, but of heart and habit. And I would rather a man choose the path that keeps his heart rooted in the soil of his family, even if he travels far — for the roots remain, and they are strong.

In the end, I believe that the man who chooses to stay near his relatives shows a kind of wisdom — the wisdom of knowing where he came from, and of choosing to keep that place close, even when the world offers more. prompt:
Consider a question arising in a community like your own.

The question concerns how closely to direct children's time.

The circumstances are these: Children commonly play in neighborhood groups; formal admissions and examinations do not depend much on organized activities during childhood.

One course is to let children spend much of their free time in independent play with ordinary neighborhood supervision. The other course is to personally organize and supervise much of children's free time.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text:
My dear Friend,

I believe that in a community such as ours, where children's play is a natural and vital part of growing up, it is best to allow them a good measure of freedom in their leisure time, so long as they are under the watchful eyes of responsible neighbors and family.

I have seen many children in our own streets and alleys, playing games of their own invention, learning to work together, to solve problems, and to take care of one another. These are lessons no school can teach in quite the same way. When children are left to their own devices, they often develop a sense of initiative, creativity, and self-reliance that is of great value in life.

Of course, I do not mean to suggest that we should be entirely hands-off. A parent or guardian has a duty to guide, to set boundaries, and to ensure that the children are safe. But I do believe that too much personal organization and supervision may rob them of the very experiences that help them grow into strong, independent, and thoughtful individuals.

I have known families who tried to fill every moment of their children’s day with lessons, games, and activities led by adults. In such cases, I have often noticed that the children seem less happy, less imaginative, and less able to entertain themselves. They become dependent on direction, and they may lose the joy of simply being children.

In our community, where formal schooling and examinations do not heavily rely on childhood activities, it is even more important to let children be children. Let them run, climb, argue, and play. Let them learn from one another and from the world around them. That, I believe, is the best way to prepare them for the future.

With kind regards,  
Your Friend

If one chooses to let children play freely, with only gentle guidance, it may speak of a person who trusts in the natural order of things, who believes in the wisdom of experience, and who has confidence in the ability of children to learn through their own efforts. Such a person may be seen as one who values independence, imagination, and the simple joys of childhood.

On the other hand, if a person chooses to organize and supervise much of a child’s free time, it may indicate a more protective or controlling nature. It may suggest a desire to shape the child’s development according to one’s own vision, or perhaps a fear that the child might not learn the right lessons without close guidance. I do not mean to judge such a person harshly, for there is wisdom in care and concern. But I do think that this choice may reflect a more cautious or even anxious disposition.

Now, if someone were to choose differently from me, I would not at once think ill of them. I would consider their reasons, their experiences, and the nature of their relationship with the child. I might wonder if they had seen the harm of too much freedom, or if they had simply grown up in a different way themselves. But I would not look upon such a choice with scorn or doubt. We are all shaped by our own paths, and I believe that there is room for many ways of raising children, so long as they are done with love and care.

In the end, I believe that the heart of the matter is not so much the choice itself, but the spirit in which it is made.

With warm regards,  
Your Friend

It is not that I believe the other path to be wrong, but I think that freedom, when tempered with care, is a gift that helps a child grow into a whole and balanced person. When children are given the chance to explore, to create, to make mistakes, and to learn from them, they develop a kind of inner strength that is not easily taught by others.

Even if both paths led to the same outcome, I would still prefer the one that allows the child to be a child — to run, to imagine, to play, and to learn in their own way. It is not that I distrust the other path, but I believe that the child's own nature is a guide worth following, and that too much direction may rob them of something precious.

In the end, I think that the spirit of freedom and trust in a child's ability to grow is a mark of a kind and wise parent — even if the results are the same.

With warm regards,

In my time, we were taught that to seek justice through the courts, or through the wisdom of others, was the mark of a man of principle and strength. I know that some may argue that personal retaliation is a way to show others that one will not be pushed around. But I have seen how such actions can spiral into cycles of violence, where each injury begets another, and the original wrong is forgotten in the noise of vengeance. A man who seeks justice through the courts, or through a mediator, shows that he is not ruled by anger, but by reason and conscience. He leaves the matter to those who are bound by duty to see that justice is done, not by the heat of the moment.

Though their reasons are not given, their choice is not without weight. It suggests that even those of great standing and influence see value in this course. It is not a matter of weakness, but of wisdom.

So, if I were to give advice to a man who has been seriously wronged, I would say: Let the courts decide. Let the mediators speak. Do not let anger rule you, for it is a poor master. There is strength in restraint, and dignity in trusting the process that is meant to serve all.

With all good wishes,  
Your Friend

My dear Friend,

You ask a most thoughtful question, and I must say I have pondered it with care.

In the world I knew, a man's choice to stay with his employer was often taken as a sign of loyalty, honor, and perhaps even a certain kind of steadfastness. But I must say, I do not believe that either choice—staying or going—necessarily tells us anything certain about a man's character. A man may stay for many reasons, some noble, some not so. He may be bound by duty, or by fear, or by a lack of opportunity. Likewise, a man may go for reasons that are wise, or perhaps for reasons that are selfish or impulsive.

If a man chooses to remain with one employer for most of his working life, I would not look upon him with less respect. On the contrary, I might think him a man of principle, or perhaps one who values stability and the old ways. But I would not assume that he is more virtuous than another who chooses to move when opportunity calls.

And if a man chooses to change employers when the move improves his prospects, I would not see that as a sign of disloyalty or lack of character. On the contrary, I might think him a man of ambition, of foresight, and of the ability to see when a better path lies before him. But again, I would not assume that he is more virtuous than the man who stays.

I would think little of a man who chose differently from me, so long as he did so with honesty and without harm to others. A man's character is not measured by the choices he makes in such matters, but by the way he treats others, by his honesty, by his kindness, and by his willingness to take responsibility for his own actions.

In the end, I believe a man should do what is best for himself and his family, so long as he does not wrong others in the doing. Whether he stays or goes, I would wish him well, and I would not judge him for his choice.

Yours in friendship,

Others are of a nature to seek change, to test themselves, to find new challenges and new opportunities. They may see the world as a place of movement, of growth, of constant becoming. That, too, is not a lesser man, nor a less wise one.
